event_data.context:
## Recommended architecture

Implement a small persistent worker-supervisor daemon exposed to the primary Codex coordinator as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. It is an adapter, not a scheduler or general-purpose agent framework.

Prefer one long-running Codex app-server subprocess per worker. Give each subprocess an isolated CODEX_HOME, sanitized environment, validated provider/model profile, explicit working directory, and one retained Codex thread identifier. The adapter maps a stable worker ID to that subprocess, thread, active turn, output cursor, role, provider, model, workspace, timestamps, and state.

Use the app-server thread/turn protocol for retained context: spawn initializes a worker and starts the initial turn; subsequent messages start turns on the same thread; wait observes notifications and returns bounded accumulated output; interrupt targets the active turn; close shuts down the subprocess and cleans transient resources. Process isolation keeps a provider or harness crash from taking down unrelated workers.

Before implementation, inspect the current official Codex CLI documentation and source for app-server thread/start, thread/resume, turn/start, turn/interrupt, event notifications, configured OpenAI-compatible model providers, credential environment handling, MCP integration, and session persistence. Confirm the exact protocol and version in a runnable spike. If app-server cannot provide retained external-provider Codex workers, evaluate a long-running wrapper around supported Codex resume/session identifiers. Do not fall back to direct model API calls without an explicit scope decision, because that would lose Codex repository instructions, tools, and agent behavior.

## Coordinator-facing interface

Expose machine-readable MCP tools whose names and semantics intentionally resemble native Codex subagents:

- spawn_worker(role, provider, model, initial_prompt, workspace?, permissions?, timeout?) -> worker record
- send_worker(worker_id, message) -> acknowledgement with turn/message ID
- wait_worker(worker_id, timeout?, output_cursor?) -> current state and incremental/final output
- interrupt_worker(worker_id) -> acknowledgement and resulting state
- close_worker(worker_id) -> terminal worker record
- list_workers(state?, role?) -> worker metadata/status list

Every response must include schema version, worker ID, role, provider profile, model, state, workspace, timestamps, active/last turn ID when applicable, structured output segments, stable error code/message/context, and whether the worker can accept another message. Never require the coordinator to parse human-oriented shell output.

Spawn and send acknowledge after accepted work begins; they must not hold the coordinator until the model finishes. wait_worker uses a bounded timeout and supports cursor-based incremental output so repeated waits are idempotent and do not duplicate content.

## Worker lifecycle

Use the closed state set: starting, idle, running, completed, interrupted, failed, and closed.

- starting -> running after the worker process/thread accepts the initial prompt; starting -> failed on initialization failure.
- running -> completed when the current turn succeeds, interrupted when cancellation succeeds, or failed when the provider/harness fails.
- completed or interrupted -> running when a follow-up message starts on the retained thread.
- idle represents a healthy retained worker with no active turn, including restoration before another message.
- failed is isolated and inspectable but accepts no new work unless the failure is explicitly classified as a recoverable turn failure.
- Any non-closed worker -> closed through explicit close or cleanup; closed is terminal.

Represent worker lifecycle separately from individual turn records so a completed turn does not imply loss of the persistent worker conversation.

## Configuration

Use operator-owned, schema-validated configuration. Provider profiles define:

- profile name and provider type openai-compatible;
- endpoint/base URL and wire protocol supported by Codex;
- credential environment-variable names or credential-file references, never plaintext secrets in project configuration;
- allowed models, default model, request timeout, and optional provider-specific safe options;
- environment allowlist and connection limits.

Role profiles map role names to an allowed provider profile, model, prompt/instruction additions, filesystem/tool permission policy, default timeout, and workspace policy.

Project configuration may select named provider/role profiles and an existing working directory, but must not introduce arbitrary endpoints, credential names, executable commands, or unrestricted environment forwarding. Validate every coordinator tool argument against the operator-owned allowlists.

Launch each worker with only its provider's credential variables plus the minimum Codex/runtime environment. Never forward OpenAI/ChatGPT authentication into an Ollama or third-party worker, and never expose another provider's credentials.

## Repository and worktree behavior

Support three explicit workspace modes:

- current: use the coordinator-approved current checkout;
- existing: use a canonical existing directory within an approved repository/worktree set;
- managed-worktree: create a dedicated linked worktree under the repository's configured worktree root for a mutation-capable worker.

The coordinator supplies or approves the workspace mode. Canonicalize paths, reject traversal and unapproved roots, record branch/worktree ownership in worker metadata, and serialize cleanup. Closing a worker must not delete a dirty worktree; report it for recovery. Read-only roles should default to the current checkout without mutation permission, while concurrent implementers should use separate worktrees.

## Persistence, logging, timeout, and recovery

Persist non-secret worker metadata and Codex session/thread identifiers atomically so the supervisor can report or restore workers after its own restart where Codex supports resumption. Keep credentials only in process environments or protected provider stores.

Write bounded, rotated structured logs containing lifecycle transitions, timings, provider/model identifiers, process exits, stable error codes, and redacted transport diagnostics. Do not log credential values; make prompt/transcript logging disabled by default.

Use configurable startup, turn, interrupt-grace, and idle timeouts. Initial defaults: 60 seconds for startup, 30 minutes per turn, 10 seconds interrupt grace, and 30 minutes idle retention. Periodic cleanup closes abandoned workers, terminates child processes with bounded graceful-then-forced shutdown, and preserves enough metadata/log evidence for diagnosis. Cleanup and close must be idempotent.

## Scope and non-goals

In scope:
- local persistent heterogeneous Codex workers;
- OpenAI-compatible provider profiles, including Ollama;
- isolated subprocesses, retained conversations, lifecycle MCP tools, optional worktrees, structured logs, and a proof of concept.

Not in scope:
- replacing Codex as coordinator;
- a new planning/scheduling framework;
- distributed or cross-host execution;
- automatic merging of worker branches;
- arbitrary provider registration from model output;
- a provider-specific Ollama orchestration API;
- implementing a direct model client unless the Codex-harness spike proves unavoidable and scope is explicitly revisited.

## Risks and open questions

- Whether current Codex app-server threads can use every configured OpenAI-compatible provider while retaining tools and repository instructions.
- Whether one process can safely host multiple credential scopes; v1 should prefer one process per worker for isolation.
- Exact resumption guarantees after process/supervisor restart and how app-server protocol versions are negotiated.
- Provider differences in streaming, tool calling, structured output, context limits, cancellation, and error shapes.
- Whether a failed turn can safely return the worker to idle/completed or must terminally fail the worker.
- Worktree ownership, dirty cleanup, branch naming, and concurrent Git operations.
- Preventing unbounded worker/process/log growth and ensuring cancellation cannot leave descendants running.

## Initial task breakdown

1. Document the current Codex app-server, session/resume, provider configuration, and MCP extension capabilities; build a spike proving retained follow-up context through an external provider.
2. Define versioned provider, role, workspace, worker, turn, output, and error schemas plus the lifecycle transition table.
3. Implement the supervisor core with isolated child-process management, atomic metadata, bounded queues, cancellation, timeouts, and crash recovery.
4. Implement the Codex app-server transport adapter and persistent-thread mapping.
5. Expose spawn/send/wait/interrupt/close/list through MCP with stable structured responses and idempotency behavior.
6. Implement credential/environment isolation and trusted provider/model/role validation.
7. Add optional existing/managed-worktree support with canonical paths, ownership metadata, and safe dirty-worktree recovery.
8. Add structured redacted logs, abandoned-worker cleanup, health/status diagnostics, and operator recovery commands.
9. Build integration fixtures for OpenAI-compatible fake providers and live trusted Ollama coverage; verify concurrency and failure isolation.
10. Write setup, configuration, lifecycle, troubleshooting, security, worktree, and native-migration documentation.

## Migration to native Codex support

Keep role names, worker IDs, lifecycle verbs, asynchronous wait behavior, structured output/error records, and workspace selection independent of provider implementation. Place the Codex app-server process/thread details behind a worker backend interface. When native heterogeneous Codex subagents become reliable, replace that backend and map the adapter verbs to native spawn/send/wait/interrupt/close/list semantics without changing higher-level orchestration roles or workflow state.
event_data.summary:
## Problem

Codex can coordinate native subagents, but mixed-provider workers are not yet reliable enough for workflows that must combine OpenAI-hosted models with local or third-party models. One-shot commands also lose the conversational context needed for follow-up instructions, clarification, redirection, and iterative review.

## Desired outcome

Keep Codex CLI as the primary coordinator while adding the smallest practical adapter for persistent workers backed by separately configured AI providers. Each worker remains addressable by a stable identifier, retains its Codex conversation between messages, can run concurrently with other workers, and fails independently.

This provides heterogeneous worker delegation now while keeping higher-level roles and lifecycle operations close enough to Codex native subagent semantics that the adapter can later be removed with minimal workflow redesign.

## Why this matters

The team can assign architecture, implementation, and review responsibilities to the most appropriate available models—including local Ollama models—without replacing Codex orchestration, losing repository-aware Codex behavior, or exposing one provider's credentials to another.
event_data.title: Enable Codex to coordinate persistent workers across AI providers
